name: Mazu (Goddess of the Sea)
domain: Guardian of the seas, safe voyages, protector of all people
description: Every year in the third lunar month, a human river stretches along the roads of central Taiwan: hundreds of thousands of people following a single palanquin for nine days and eight nights, more than 300 kilometers on foot. The one riding inside is Mazu — formally the Heavenly Holy Mother, affectionately called 'Mazu Po' by her devotees. She was born Lin Mo-niang, a fisherman's daughter on Meizhou Island in Fujian during the Northern Song dynasty. In life she saved countless people and could foresee storms; after her death, coastal communities enshrined her as the guardian of the sea. Ming and Qing settlers who risked their lives crossing the Taiwan Strait held on to that faith, and when they landed safely they built temples to give thanks — which is why Mazu temples stand in coastal towns all over Taiwan. Today her care reaches far beyond the water: fishermen pray for safety, merchants for business, students for exam results, and some come asking for a spouse or a child. People say Mazu is like a shared mother to the Taiwanese, and once you've seen the crowds of 'March Mazu fever,' it doesn't sound like an exaggeration.
story:
The most heart-wrenching scene in her legend takes place at a loom. Lin Mo-niang was weaving one day when she suddenly closed her eyes and slumped over the loom, her face like someone gone very far away. Out at sea a storm had broken, and the boats of her father and brother were in danger. With her spiritual power she had gone out to rescue them — one hand gripping her father, her teeth clenched on her brother's clothes. Her mother, seeing her unconscious, shook her awake in a panic. The moment Lin Mo-niang opened her mouth to speak, the brother she held in her teeth sank beneath the waves. Her father came home safely; her brother never did.

Lin Mo-niang was born in 960, the first year of the Jianlong era of the Northern Song. A bright child, she could read the scriptures by the age of eight, and for years she stood by the shore watching the sky and guiding fishing boats away from storms. In 987, the fourth year of the Yongxi era, at the age of 28, she passed away in meditation on the summit of Meiyu on Meizhou Island. Grateful villagers built a temple in her honor, and successive imperial courts kept raising her titles — from 'Lady' and 'Heavenly Consort' all the way to 'Empress of Heaven' and 'Heavenly Holy Mother.' A fisherman's daughter who could not save her own brother became the guardian of the entire Chinese seafaring world.
worship:
Offerings to Mazu are mainly vegetarian: fresh flowers, four kinds of fruit, longevity peaches, red tortoise cakes, and fa gao (prosperity cakes) are all good choices. Mazu likes cleanliness, so keep the offering table neat. How to pray: on entering the temple, first offer incense at the Heaven censer, then go before Mazu's main altar and tell her your name, your address, and what you are asking for — safe voyages, career, marriage, and children are all fine to ask about.

The 23rd day of the third lunar month is Mazu's birthday, and for weeks before and after it, processions and pilgrimages run across Taiwan. If you want to experience it yourself, walk a stretch with the Dajia Mazu or Baishatun Mazu pilgrimage and bow respectfully as the palanquin passes — one of the moments of blessing Taiwanese people cherish most.
festivals: Mazu's birthday on the 23rd day of the third lunar month is Taiwan's biggest religious occasion. The nine-day, eight-night pilgrimage procession of Dajia Zhenlan Temple and the walking pilgrimage of Baishatun Gongtian Temple draw hundreds of thousands of devotees every year, and are counted alongside the Christmas Mass at the Vatican and the pilgrimage to Mecca as one of the world's three great religious events. The Mazu procession of Beigang Chaotian Temple is famous for its spectacular folk performance troupes.

temples.name: Dajia Zhenlan Temple
temples.deityStory: The Dajia Mazu pilgrimage is Taiwan's grandest religious event, hailed as one of the 'world's three great religious events' — nine days and eight nights, more than 300 kilometers on foot.

temples.name: Beigang Chaotian Temple
temples.deityStory: A major center of Mazu worship in Taiwan, with branch temples all over the world.

temples.name: Baishatun Gongtian Temple
temples.deityStory: Baishatun Mazu is famous as the 'Pink Supercar.' The pilgrimage route is never fixed — it follows wherever Mazu's palanquin leads, a sign of how close and responsive she is to her people.

temples.name: Lugang Tianhou Temple
temples.deityStory: Enshrines the Mazu statue that crossed the strait from Meizhou with Shi Lang's forces in 1683 (known as 'Meizhou Mazu'). It is the only temple in Taiwan that houses the founding Holy Mother statue from the Meizhou ancestral temple.

temples.name: Taitung Tianhou Temple
temples.deityStory: Completed in 1891, it was the last official temple built in Taiwan during the Qing dynasty, and is the only government-built Mazu temple in eastern Taiwan.

temples.name: Songshan Ciyou Temple
temples.deityStory: Founded in the Qianlong era of the Qing dynasty, it is the most important Mazu temple in Songshan and the spiritual center beside Raohe Night Market.

temples.name: Taichung Lecheng Temple
temples.deityStory: Popularly called the 'Hanxi Mazu Temple,' it was founded in the Qianlong era of the Qing dynasty and has more than 200 years of history — an important center of Mazu worship in Taichung. Its Yue Lao (matchmaker god) is also said to be very responsive.

temples.name: Changhua Nanyao Temple
temples.deityStory: Changhua's most important Mazu temple, with its own distinctive 'Bengang pilgrimage' tradition, a long history, and beautiful architecture.

temples.name: Shanbian Mazu Temple
temples.deityStory: For many years Shanbian Mazu was 'a deity without a temple,' enshrined in the home of whichever incense master (luzhu) was serving that year. Only in recent years was a Mazu temple completed.

temples.name: Tainan Grand Mazu Temple
temples.deityStory: Originally the residence of the Ming Prince of Ningjing, it was converted into a Tianhou temple in the Kangxi era of the Qing dynasty. It is Taiwan's first government-built Mazu temple, and was entered into the official state sacrifices in 1720.

temples.name: Xingang Fengtian Temple
temples.deityStory: One of Chiayi's most important Mazu temples, known as the destination of the Dajia Mazu procession, and always thronged with worshippers.

temples.name: Hualien Gang Tian Temple
temples.deityStory: The most important Mazu temple in the Hualien area, watching over the fishermen and residents of the east coast.

temples.name: Matsu Tianhou Temple
temples.deityStory: Legend says Mazu's body drifted ashore here and the islanders built a temple to her. This is how the Matsu Islands got their name, and it is an important sacred site of Mazu worship.

temples.name: Penghu Tianhou Temple
temples.deityStory: The oldest Mazu temple in Taiwan, already standing in the Ming dynasty, and the most important center of faith in Penghu.

name: Guan Sheng Di Jun (Lord Guan)
domain: Martial god of wealth, god of loyalty, righteousness, and keeping one's word
description: Walk down any old street in Taiwan and look up at the shop shrines — the figure presiding there is often the red-faced, long-bearded Guan Sheng Dijun, better known as Guan Gong or Enzhu Gong. He was once Guan Yu, the great general of the Three Kingdoms era, whose Green Dragon Crescent Blade won him a reputation that has lasted a thousand years. In Taiwan today he may be the busiest god of all: business owners worship him as the martial god of wealth, scholars pray to him for exam luck (Guan Gong was never without his copy of the Spring and Autumn Annals), and police officers and merchants pray to him for integrity and fairness. Rarer still, he is a historical figure honored by three traditions at once — folk religion reveres him as the 'Martial Sage,' Taoism as 'Xie Tian Da Di,' and Buddhism as the Sangharama Bodhisattva. From Taipei's Xingtian Temple to Tainan's Grand Martial Temple, his incense has burned for a thousand years, sustained not by force of arms but by a single word: righteousness.
story:
Cao Cao may be history's most frustrated fan. After he had Guan Yu surrounded and brought him over to his side, he gave him fine wine and food, high rank and rich salary, and even the finest horse in the land, Red Hare. Guan Yu accepted Red Hare and was unmoved by everything else. Only one thing was on his mind: where was his sworn elder brother, Liu Bei?

The moment word came, Guan Yu set off, escorting his two sisters-in-law. Cao Cao had five passes along the way set to stop him, and he fought his way through every one — the episode told for a thousand years as 'crossing five passes and slaying six generals.' He turned his back on wealth and glory laid out before him, choosing instead to ride alone across a thousand li to join a brother who had nothing at the time.

This kind of loyalty, which holds a promise dearer than life, is exactly why Taiwanese people have stayed devoted to him for generations. In business, what people fear most is someone who won't keep their word — so they entrust their business to the god who keeps his word above all.
worship:
What is Guan Sheng Dijun best to pray for? Wealth and honest dealing in business, success in exams, fairness and justice, and warding off evil — all fall within his jurisdiction.

How to pray: set out your offerings, offer incense, state your name and what you are asking for, and finally cast the moon blocks (bwa bwei) to ask whether the god grants it. What matters most is sincerity — Guan Gong can't stand hypocrites.

Offerings: the three sacrificial meats (a whole chicken, pork, and a whole fish), longevity peaches, longevity noodles, and three cups of tea. Some people also place a copy of the Spring and Autumn Annals on the table as a tribute.

There is only one taboo, but it's the most important: keep your heart upright. If you're after shady windfalls, don't waste the incense — Guan Gong won't tolerate it.
festivals: Guan Sheng Dijun's birthday on the 24th day of the sixth lunar month is his most important festival. Guandi temples across Taiwan, including Taipei's Xingtian Temple and Tainan's Grand Martial Temple, hold grand celebrations with Taoist rites, fire-walking ceremonies, and opera performances for the gods.

temples.name: Xingtian Temple
temples.deityStory: In 2014 the temple removed its incense burners and offering tables and switched to incense-free worship. It is also known as a good place for shoujing, the rite for calming a frightened spirit.

temples.name: Tainan Grand Martial Temple
temples.deityStory: The only martial temple in Taiwan listed in the official state sacrifices, with more than 300 years of history — step inside and you can feel its solemn presence.

temples.name: Jiaoxi Sietian Temple
temples.deityStory: Soak in the hot springs, then pay your respects to Guan Gong — this is Yilan's most important center of Guandi worship.

associatedTemples: Xingtian Temple (Taipei City)
Tainan Grand Martial Temple (Tainan City)
Jiaoxi Sietian Temple (Yilan County)

name: Earth God (Tu Di Gong)
aliases: Fude Zhengshen (Righteous God of Fortune and Virtue)
domain: Guardian of the land, wealth and good harvests, neighborhood peace
description: In Taiwan, Tudigong shrines are everywhere — beside the fields, at the mouth of the lane, at the foot of the hills. This white-bearded old gentleman's formal title is Fude Zhengshen, but everyone calls him Tudigong or Tudi Bo, which sounds like the kindest uncle in the neighborhood. He looks after the most down-to-earth matters: a safe home, a good harvest, harmony among neighbors, and a wallet that isn't too thin — you could fairly call him the neighborhood chief of the spirit world. His shrines may be small, but no god is more tightly woven into Taiwanese life. Business owners worship him on the 2nd and 16th of every lunar month in a rite called 'zuo ya,' and the last zuo ya of the year is 'weiya' — the origin of today's year-end company banquet for employees. From tiny roadside shrines to the queues at Nantou's Zinan Temple, this most unassuming of gods is the one the Taiwanese can least do without.
story:
The most widely told version goes like this: in the Zhou dynasty there was a tax official named Zhang Fude, so honest that he gave his own salary to help the poor. He lived to 102 — a true super-centenarian by ancient standards.

After he died, a farmer who had benefited from his kindness built a simple little shrine out of three stones to worship him. Then something strange happened: the farmer started to prosper. Word spread, neighbors rushed to follow his example, and Tudigong shrines went up one after another — perhaps the most successful word-of-mouth marketing in history.

An honest official who, after death, got his start with three stones and became one of the gods the Taiwanese know best. No dazzling miracles, just the simplest truth: good people are rewarded. That's what makes Tudigong so lovable — he isn't distant or forbidding, but like an old neighbor who watched you grow up.
worship:
What do you pray to Tudigong for? Wealth (he's the most approachable god of fortune), a safe home, thriving business, and good harvests. Business owners, take note: on the 2nd and 16th of every lunar month you 'zuo ya' — make offerings to him. That's the old rule.

How to pray is simple — the offerings needn't be lavish. The three sacrificial meats, fruit, peanuts, mochi, and candy all work; Tudigong isn't picky, and sincerity matters most. When you offer incense, state your address, your name, and what you are asking for. If you're praying for wealth, you can burn 'Tudigong joss paper,' or go to Zinan Temple in Zhushan, Nantou, and cast the moon blocks to borrow 'fortune money' to use as seed money.

There's only one taboo: if you borrow fortune money, you must go back and repay it (Zinan Temple's rule is to return it the following year). Tudigong is very kind — and he also has a very good memory.
festivals: Tudigong's birthday on the 2nd day of the second lunar month (the 'first ya' of the year) is celebrated at Tudigong temples everywhere, alongside the prayers for peace that follow the Lantern Festival. The 16th day of the twelfth lunar month is 'weiya,' the last zuo ya of the year. Traditionally, the boss would host a banquet for employees on this day; if the chicken's head was pointed at an employee, it hinted that they would not be kept on the next year. This custom evolved into the modern company 'weiya banquet,' a year-end tradition unique to Taiwan.

temples.name: Zhushan Zinan Temple
temples.deityStory: Famous across Taiwan for its 'fortune money' loans. If the moon blocks give approval, devotees can borrow money from Tudigong as start-up capital — said to be remarkably effective — and repay it the following year.

temples.name: Checheng Fu'an Temple
temples.deityStory: The largest Tudigong temple in Southeast Asia, with grand architecture. Most remarkable is its joss paper furnace, nicknamed the 'divine money-counting machine': place joss paper at the vent and it is drawn in automatically — quite a sight.

temples.name: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple
temples.deityStory: Northern Taiwan's best-known place to pray for wealth, with a giant Tudigong statue. Its hilltop setting offers sweeping views, making it a great spot for night scenery, and it is open for worship 24 hours a day.

associatedTemples: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple (Zhonghe District, New Taipei City)
Checheng Fu'an Temple (Checheng Township, Pingtung County)

name: Jade Emperor (Yu Huang Da Di)
domain: Ruler of the heavenly court, head of all gods, sovereign of heaven and earth
description: Late on the night of the 9th day of the first lunar month, many Taiwanese households stay up. When the zi hour arrives, offering tables are set out in the open air and whole families perform the solemn rite of three kneelings and nine prostrations toward the sky. This is 'Tiangong Sheng,' the birthday of the Jade Emperor — known to the Taiwanese as Tiangong or Tiangong Zu. He is the highest-ranking deity in Taoism, ruling the three realms of heaven, earth, and water and governing all immortals and every living thing in the human world. Wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and the turning of the seasons are his to direct; the good and evil, fortune and misfortune of the human world come under his review; and at year's end the gods all ascend to the heavenly court to report to him. When Taiwanese people feel wronged, they look up and cry 'Tiangong Bo!' and a common saying goes, 'Tiangong looks after good people' — whether or not they ever set foot in a temple, Tiangong has long lived in the Taiwanese language. To see a lively Tiangong Sheng, head to the Tainan Tiantan: lights blaze all night and firecrackers never stop.
story:
According to Taoist scriptures, the Jade Emperor was once the crown prince of the Kingdom of Guangyan Miaole. Compassionate from childhood, he ruled the kingdom well after taking the throne — and then, at the height of his glory, gave up the throne and went deep into the mountains to cultivate the Tao. He cultivated for 1,750 kalpas, each kalpa lasting 129,600 years, and then went through an even longer period of cultivation before attaining the position of Jade Emperor and ruling the three realms. Even the supreme Lord of Heaven had to earn his place step by step through hard cultivation; no one is simply born to sit on that throne.

Folk belief has a version closer to everyday life: every year on the 25th day of the twelfth lunar month, the Jade Emperor comes down in person to inspect the good and evil of the human world. People are especially careful in word and deed that day, because 'Tiangong is watching.' In an age without security cameras, that phrase was Taiwanese society's earliest system of self-discipline — even if no one sees, someone in heaven is keeping track.
worship:
Worshipping Tiangong is the most formal of all rites, and nothing can be done carelessly. The offering table is set outdoors facing the sky, in two tiers. The top table is for Tiangong: fresh flowers, candles, three cups of tea, five fruits, six vegetarian dishes, sweet rice cake, and red glutinous rice balls. The lower table is for Tiangong's attendants, with the five sacrificial meats. Two stalks of sugarcane tied with red string stand beside the table, symbolizing rising 'joint by joint.' The joss paper must be the highest grade, 'Tiangong gold.'

Timing matters too: on the 9th day of the first lunar month, 'Tiangong Sheng,' worship begins at the zi hour (11 p.m.) with the rite of three kneelings and nine prostrations — the most solemn ceremony of the year. The taboo with Tiangong lies in your attitude: only reverence will do. Offerings and rites may be simple, but never casual.
festivals: 'Tiangong Sheng' on the 9th day of the first lunar month is one of Taiwan's most important religious festivals. The 25th day of the twelfth lunar month, when the heavenly gods descend, is another important day: Tiangong inspects the good and evil of the human world, a day folk tradition calls 'Tiangong coming down to earth.'

temples.name: Tainan Tiantan (Altar of Heaven)
temples.deityStory: Popularly called the 'Tiangong Temple,' it was built in 1854 with funds pooled by the officials and people of the prefectural city, and is billed as 'Taiwan's foremost temple.' Its 'One' (一) plaque is one of Tainan's three famous plaques, symbolizing that 'however carefully you calculate, it can't match Heaven's single reckoning.'

temples.name: Songshan Fengtian Temple
temples.deityStory: A large-scale Tiangong temple in Taipei, busy with worshippers. Its imposing architecture makes it an important place for devotees to pray for safety and the removal of misfortune.

name: Yue Lao (Old Man Under the Moon)
domain: Matchmaking, tying the red thread, bringing about happy marriages
description: Before Valentine's Day, the line at Taipei's Xia-Hai City God Temple can wind right out of the temple courtyard — everyone in it has come to see the Old Man Under the Moon. This god, affectionately called Yue Lao or Yue Lao Gong, has only one line of business: love and marriage. In his hands is a marriage register recording who is destined for whom; once he ties the red thread, two people will find their way to each other however far apart they are. In Taiwan, Yue Lao's popularity is astonishing: on Qixi, on Valentine's Day, and on ordinary weekends, singles line up at the major Yue Lao temples to ask for a red thread, and even visitors from Japan fly in specially to pray. Just look at the wedding cakes brought back to Xia-Hai City God Temple in thanks — the temple counts more than 6,000 couples returning each year — and you can see how impressive the old man's 'match success rate' is. However advanced technology gets, the most powerful dating algorithm in Taiwanese hearts is still the red thread in Yue Lao's hand.
story:
Yue Lao's most famous appearance came on a moonlit night in the Tang dynasty. A scholar named Wei Gu, outside an inn, came across a white-bearded old man leafing through a large book by the light of the moon. Curious, Wei Gu asked what it was. The old man said, 'This is the marriage register of everyone under heaven.'

Wei Gu eagerly asked about his own marriage. The old man flipped a few pages and pointed to a little girl in the arms of an old woman across the street: 'That's her.' Wei Gu looked — small and grubby, nothing like what he had imagined. He was so angry that he sent someone to kill her. The assassin couldn't bring himself to do it and only left a cut between the girl's eyebrows.

Fourteen years later, Wei Gu married a beautiful wife. On their wedding night he noticed a scar between her brows, and when he asked — she was that very girl.

Fourteen years of running, a long way around, and he still ended up at the other end of the red thread. The story has been told for a thousand years, and it says one thing: the red thread Yue Lao ties can't be cut, not even with a blade.
worship:
What do you ask Yue Lao for? Finding a partner, a good match, a smooth relationship. Note: Yue Lao only handles 'true matches' — if you want to break up a couple or take someone else's partner, he won't take the case.

How to pray: first introduce yourself to Yue Lao (name, birthday, address, and your current relationship status), then sincerely describe the qualities of your ideal partner — be specific, but don't go overboard. Then ask for a red thread, put it in your wallet and keep it with you; don't wash it or lose it until you meet the right person.

Recommended offerings: red dates, longans, peanuts, and lotus seeds — together a pun on 'may you soon have a precious child' — plus some candy to keep the relationship sweet.

The most important taboo: don't bring an umbrella when you pray to Yue Lao — the word for 'umbrella' sounds like 'to break apart.' Once you've found your match, remember to bring your partner back to give thanks with wedding cakes; that's what Yue Lao loves to see most.
festivals: Yue Lao has no particular birthday celebration, but every year around Qixi (the 7th day of the seventh lunar month, the Chinese Valentine's Day) and Valentine's Day on February 14, the crowds at the major Yue Lao temples multiply several times over.

temples.name: Taipei Xia-Hai City God Temple
temples.deityStory: The Yue Lao here is famous. According to the temple's 2017 count, more than 6,000 couples come back each year with wedding cakes to give thanks — an astonishing rate.

temples.name: Manka Longshan Temple
temples.deityStory: Longshan Temple's Yue Lao sits in the rear hall and is just as popular. Many young people, after paying respects to Guanyin, make a special trip to the rear hall to ask for a red thread.

temples.name: Taichung Lecheng Temple
temples.deityStory: The media has called Lecheng Temple's Yue Lao hall one of the most responsive Yue Lao temples in Taichung, and many singles come because of its reputation.

temples.name: Tainan Grand Mazu Temple
temples.deityStory: The Yue Lao at Tainan Grand Mazu Temple is one of the most responsive matchmaking gods in the old city of Tainan, drawing large numbers of devotees every year to ask for a red thread.

temples.name: Tainan Grand Martial Temple
temples.deityStory: The Yue Lao at the Grand Martial Temple is known for being effective at 'cutting peach blossoms' — helping devotees sever unhealthy romantic entanglements.

associatedTemples: Manka Longshan Temple (Wanhua District, Taipei City)
Taipei Xia-Hai City God Temple (Datong District, Taipei City)
Taichung Lecheng Temple (East District, Taichung City)

Tainan Grand Martial Temple (West Central District, Tainan City)

name: City God (Cheng Huang)
domain: Protecting the city and its people, justice in the underworld, rewarding good and punishing evil
description: At the entrance of Tainan's Prefectural City God Temple hangs a plaque that reads 'So You've Come.' For people with a clear conscience it feels like a warm welcome; for those with something to hide, it sends a chill down the spine. This is the City God (Chenghuang Ye), also called Chenghuang Laoye or Chenghuang Zunshen — the local magistrate of the underworld. The living world has mayors and county magistrates; the underworld has the City God. Wrongs you got away with in life are all on his books, one entry at a time. He is judge, prosecutor, and police chief of the underworld rolled into one, and the giant abacus in his temple is his signature: in the end, every deed is accounted for. But the City God doesn't only inspire fear — he also protects the peace of his district, and there is even a ranking system: a Du Chenghuang oversees a province, a Fu Chenghuang a prefecture, and a Xian Chenghuang a county, matching the ranks of the living bureaucracy exactly. The Hsinchu City God Temple is the highest-ranking in Taiwan. Crowded with worshippers by day, full of atmosphere by night — that coexistence of the living and the dead is a charm only City God temples have.
story:
The City God actually has no single fixed identity. Each locality's City God is usually someone from that place who was upright and respected in life and took up the post after death — so Taipei's City God and Tainan's City God are not the same person at all. The system itself, in which good people become officials after death, is deeply moving: live an honest life, and one day it might be your turn to guard a piece of land and its people.

What the temples share is how they're arranged. Some hang a 'So You've Come' plaque at the entrance (the one at Tainan's Prefectural City God Temple is the most famous), like a greeting that has been waiting for you a long time. Inside the hall hangs a giant abacus, reminding you that every account is being kept. On either side stand the tall and the short, the white and the black — General Xie and General Fan, known in folk belief as Black and White Impermanence — whose job is to round up those due to report to the underworld. As a child, led into a City God temple by the grown-ups, you couldn't look those two towering statues in the eye. Only when you grow up do you understand: what you feared was never the statues, but the ledger in your own heart.
worship:
What do you ask the City God for? Fairness and justice (many people come before a court case), protection from people who would do you harm, and peace for the community. The Yue Lao at many City God temples is also famously responsive — Taipei's Xia-Hai City God Temple receives thank-you wedding cakes by the thousands every year.

How to pray: bring the three sacrificial meats and wine. First offer incense at the Heaven censer, then go to the City God's main hall and state your name, your address, and what you are asking for. If you are seeking justice for a wrong, you can write down the injustice and burn it as your report. Offerings should be formal — the three meats, wine, and joss paper shouldn't be done carelessly.

The biggest taboo: never lie or swear a false oath in a City God temple. Keeping accounts is his whole job, so lying in front of him is walking straight into the net.
festivals: Festival dates differ from temple to temple. Taipei's Xia-Hai City God Temple celebrates on the 13th day of the fifth lunar month, when the City God's procession is the event of the year in Dadaocheng. The Hsinchu City God Temple holds its annual rites and procession in the seventh lunar month, and the food stalls outside the temple are famous too.

temples.name: Taipei Xia-Hai City God Temple
temples.deityStory: Although its main deity is the City God, the temple's Yue Lao is internationally famous. Every year countless couples return with wedding cakes to give thanks, making it Taiwan's most powerful place for finding a partner.

temples.name: Hualien City God Temple
temples.deityStory: Located on Chenggong Street in Hualien City, it watches over the people of eastern Taiwan.

temples.name: Hsinchu City God Temple
temples.deityStory: The highest-ranking City God temple in Taiwan (a Du Chenghuang). Its City God procession is grand in scale, and the food stalls outside the temple are famous too.

temples.name: Chiayi City God Temple
temples.deityStory: Chiayi's most important City God temple, with a long history. Its annual City God procession is a major religious event in the Chiayi area.

temples.name: Kinmen Wudao City God Temple
temples.deityStory: The most important City God temple in Kinmen, with a history going back to the Ming dynasty — the center of faith for the people of Kinmen.

name: God of Wealth (Cai Shen)
aliases: Gods of Wealth of the Five Directions
domain: Governing the world's wealth, attracting fortune, thriving business
description: In the small hours of the 5th day of the first lunar month, shops all over Taiwan are awake at almost the same moment — firecrackers go off down the street as every business reopens to 'welcome the God of Wealth.' The guest of honor is Caishen Ye, the God of Wealth. The most common in Taiwan is the martial god of wealth Zhao Gongming, also called Xuantan Zhenjun; together with four generals of the east, west, south, and north, they are known as the Gods of Wealth of the Five Directions, symbolizing money flowing in from every road. His job couldn't be more direct: money. Merchants pray for thriving business, office workers for raises and promotions, lottery players for windfall luck — and Taiwanese worship him in very practical ways: bringing bankbooks, business cards, and receipts to a wealth temple to pass them through the incense smoke for a blessing, or lining up at Zinan Temple in Zhushan, Nantou, to borrow 'fortune money' as seed money, a practice that draws several million visits a year. To soak up some wealth energy, visit Beigang Wude Palace in Yunlin, the founding temple of the Gods of Wealth of the Five Directions — its 'Heavenly Treasury' furnace, billed as the largest in the world, is impressive just to look at.
story:
The origin of the martial god of wealth Zhao Gongming is recorded in Investiture of the Gods — and he started out on the losing side.

At the end of the Shang dynasty, Zhao Gongming had cultivated the Tao on Mount Emei for many years and had mastered powerful magic. When King Wu of Zhou rose against King Zhou of Shang, Zhao was asked to come down the mountain to help the Shang. Riding a black tiger and wielding an iron whip, he left Jiang Ziya's army helpless. In the end, Jiang Ziya used a secret curse, the 'Nail-Head Seven-Arrow Scroll,' to work against him in secret, and Zhao Gongming's life force drained away until he died — a great master who fell not on the battlefield but to a hidden scheme.

When the gods were invested, Jiang Ziya weighed his life: though he had chosen the wrong side, he had been loyal and righteous and deeply versed in the Tao. So he was named 'Golden Dragon Ruyi Zhengyi Dragon-Tiger Xuantan Zhenjun,' commanding four generals — of treasure, of riches, of wealth, and of profitable trade — and placed in charge of the world's wealth.

He lost the war but won a thousand years of incense. The most important god of wealth in the Chinese world is a loyal man honored even in defeat. It's a reminder to everyone who comes asking for money: what the God of Wealth respects is wealth earned the honest way.
worship:
Offerings to the God of Wealth are all about prosperity and good omens: fa gao (for getting rich), pineapple (for fortune coming your way), tangerines (for great luck), and apples (for safety). Cakes shaped like gold ingots fit the occasion perfectly, and the joss paper should be 'God of Wealth gold.' Business owners can set out five kinds of fruit beside the cash register.

The most Taiwanese way to worship? Bring your bankbook, business cards, or receipts to a wealth temple and pass them through the incense smoke for the god's blessing. You can also go to Zinan Temple in Zhushan and cast the moon blocks to borrow 600 NT dollars in fortune money as seed money — just remember to repay it, with interest, the following year.

Key dates: the 5th day of the first lunar month, when businesses reopen to welcome the God of Wealth, and the zuo ya offerings on the 2nd and 16th of every lunar month. Honest income and career success are the right things to ask for; if you're after crooked money, don't even bother asking.
festivals: Welcoming the God of Wealth on the 5th day of the first lunar month is his most important festival. In the early hours of that day, businesses across Taiwan set off firecrackers and burn joss paper to welcome the God of Wealth into their premises. Shops choose this day to reopen for the new year, a custom known as 'po wu' (breaking the fifth), symbolizing an auspicious start to the year's work. The zuo ya offerings on the 2nd and 16th of each lunar month are also closely tied to the worship of the God of Wealth.

temples.name: Beigang Wude Palace
temples.deityStory: The founding temple of the Gods of Wealth of the Five Directions in Taiwan. Its giant 'Heavenly Treasury' furnace is billed as the largest in the world, symbolizing an overflowing treasury.

temples.name: Zhushan Zinan Temple
temples.deityStory: Although its main deity is Tudigong, its reputation for answering prayers for wealth makes it one of the most important wealth temples. The custom of borrowing fortune money keeps crowds coming all year round.

temples.name: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple
temples.deityStory: Its giant Tudigong statue has become a landmark of northern Taiwan.

associatedTemples: Beigang Wude Palace (Beigang Township, Yunlin County)

name: Wenchang Dijun (God of Culture and Literature)
domain: Studies, exam luck, scholarly and official success
description: When exam season arrives, the offering tables at Wenchang temples pile up with a small mountain of photocopied admission tickets, set beside scallions, celery, and radishes — the classic scene of Taiwanese students praying to Wenchang Dijun. Also called Wenchang Gong or Zitong Dijun, he is the god in charge of exams and scholarly success: in imperial times he decided who made the list, and today he looks after the college entrance exams, the national civil service exams, and professional certifications — anything with a score is his department. For Taiwanese students, praying to Wenchang is a standard part of exam prep, much like a Japanese student's visit to a Tenmangu shrine. And often it isn't just the student who comes: grandma, mom, and the aunties next door all come to pray on their behalf, the whole family gathered before one altar — Taiwanese family solidarity on full display at the Wenchang temple. If you pass the Taipei Wenchang Temple in Shuanglian during exam season, step inside and feel the whole-nation, final-sprint atmosphere.
story:
Wenchang Dijun is the star lord in heaven who governs 'literary fortune' — everything in the human world that has to do with learning and exams falls under his care.

The point of praying to Wenchang Dijun isn't 'pray and you'll pass.' It's that he helps people who are actually putting in the work. He's no wish-granting machine; he's more like a strict but fair teacher. Study what you're supposed to study, and he'll take care of your luck on the day. Spend the run-up playing video games, and no amount of praying will help — Wenchang Dijun can see. Of all the gods, he may be the one most like a teacher.
worship:
What do you ask Wenchang Dijun for? Every kind of exam — college entrance exams, national civil service exams, graduate school, certifications — plus better grades, promotion reviews, and getting your thesis done.

How to pray: bring a photocopy of your admission ticket, offer incense, and state your name, the type of exam, and its date and location. Then place the copy on the offering table to pass through the incense, take it home, and tuck it inside a book.

The offerings are one long string of puns: scallions (clever), celery (hardworking), radish (a good omen), rice dumplings (sure to pass), and osmanthus cake (top honors) — the humor of Taiwanese temple culture at its best.

The most important taboo: never bring duck eggs. Scoring zero is called 'getting a duck egg,' so bringing duck eggs is like praying to score zero.
festivals: The 3rd day of the second lunar month is Wenchang Dijun's birthday. At this time, and before exam seasons (such as the college entrance exams), Wenchang temples hold large prayer ceremonies in which Taoist priests light lamps of brightness for students and perform rites to 'open their wisdom' — a grand sight.

temples.name: Taipei Wenchang Temple
temples.deityStory: Right next to Shuanglian MRT Station.

temples.name: Chihkan Tower (Fort Provintia)
temples.deityStory: The Wenchang Pavilion stands within the Chihkan Tower grounds, and its second floor now enshrines Kuixing. Chihkan Tower itself is a national monument.

associatedTemples: Chihkan Tower (Fort Provintia) (West Central District, Tainan City)

name: Baosheng Dadi (Great Emperor of Life Protection)
domain: God of medicine, dispelling disaster and hardship, protector of health
description: Crouching beside many statues of Baosheng Dadi is a tiger — and it isn't decoration, it's a patient. Legend says this god of medicine, known as Dadao Gong or Wu Zhenren, once pulled a bone stuck in a tiger's throat out with his bare hands, and the grateful tiger has stayed by his side ever since. Baosheng Dadi's real name was Wu Tao (written 吳夲), a celebrated physician of Tong'an, Fujian, in the Northern Song dynasty. In life he was a gifted healer who treated everyone regardless of rank; after his death, the people of southern Fujian revered him as their most important god of medicine. Settlers brought him to Taiwan, and to this day people come to pray for health and recovery. Even doctors, nurses, and pharmacists honor him as the patron of their profession, and some temples still keep traditional 'medicine lots.' His flagship temple, Dalongdong Baoan Temple in Taipei, won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award for Cultural Heritage Conservation for its meticulous restoration — if you want to see the peak of Taiwanese temple craftsmanship, this is the place.
story:
Wu Tao's most famous house call was for the empress dowager. Legend says the mother of Emperor Renzong of Song had been ill for a long time without recovering. Wu Tao cured her, and the emperor wanted to make him an imperial physician — wealth and honor in a single step. He declined, asking only to go home and keep practicing medicine, treating poor people who couldn't afford medicine, and often buying medicine for them out of his own pocket.

He was born in 979, the fourth year of the Taiping Xingguo era of the Northern Song, in Baijiao Village, Tong'an, Fujian. He was skilled in internal and external medicine, acupuncture, and herbal remedies, and especially good at fighting epidemics. In 1036, the third year of the Jingyou era, at 58, Wu Tao lost his footing while gathering herbs in the mountains and fell to his death — a healer who fell on the road to gather medicine. Grateful villagers built a temple to him and honored him as Baosheng Dadi.

Taiwanese folklore also tells an amusing tale: Dadao Gong and Mazu were once lovers who later broke up. Every third lunar month, Dadao Gong whips up wind to mess up Mazu's hair, and Mazu sends rain to soak Dadao Gong — which is why the weather in the third month swings between wind and rain, a pattern known as 'Dadao Gong's wind, Mazu's rain.'
worship:
Worship of Baosheng Dadi values purity, and the offerings can be simple: fresh flowers, fruit, and tea are enough — sincerity is what counts. What's best to pray for? Healing, good health and safety, and the removal of misfortune — even doctors, nurses, and pharmacists come to pay respects to the patron of their profession.

Some temples offer 'medicine lots': after casting the moon blocks and drawing a lot, you take the prescription to a Chinese herbal pharmacy. These days, though, most temples remind people that medicine lots are a source of spiritual comfort — if you feel unwell, see a doctor first.

The 15th day of the third lunar month is Baosheng Dadi's birthday. Dalongdong Baoan Temple's Baosheng Cultural Festival runs for months, with family-sponsored opera, fire-walking ceremonies, and arts events, carrying the spirit of healing the world right up to the present.
festivals: For Baosheng Dadi's birthday on the 15th day of the third lunar month, Dalongdong Baoan Temple holds its Baosheng Cultural Festival, which runs for more than two months and includes family-sponsored opera, fire-walking ceremonies, and art exhibitions. Baoan Temple's 'family-surname opera' is funded in rotation by local families of different surnames as thanks to the gods, a display of community cohesion.

temples.name: Dalongdong Baoan Temple
temples.deityStory: Winner of a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award for Cultural Heritage Conservation, with exquisite temple architecture. Its annual Baosheng Cultural Festival is one of Taipei's major religious and cultural events.

associatedTemples: Dalongdong Baoan Temple (Datong District, Taipei City)

name: Xuantian Shangdi (Supreme Emperor of Dark Heaven)
aliases: Beiji Dadi (Great Emperor of the North Pole)
domain: Subduing evil and demons, protecting the nation and people, guardian of the north
description: Standing on a tortoise and a snake, hair loose, feet bare, holding a seven-star sword — that unmistakable figure is Xuantian Shangdi, the Supreme Emperor of the Dark Heaven, commonly called Shangdi Gong or Diye Gong, and also known as Zhenwu Dadi or Beiji Dadi. He holds a very high rank in Taoism, governing the seven stars of the north and occupying the seat of the Black Tortoise. In Taiwan he is known for his fierce power to drive out demons and subdue evil — when something sinister, ill-omened, or unclean happens, Shangdi Gong is the first god many people think of, and many spirit mediums and ritual masters take him as their principal deity. Every year around his birthday on the 3rd day of the third lunar month, pilgrims stream to Songboling Shoutian Temple in Nantou, the head temple with the most branch temples of Xuantian Shangdi in Taiwan. One small detail: Xuantian Shangdi belongs to the north, whose element is water, and the color of water is black — so his statues and temples are mostly in black tones. Look for it next time you visit.
story:
The most widely told version is the story of a butcher.

Legend says that in a past life Xuantian Shangdi was a butcher who had taken many lives. One day an immortal enlightened him; he woke up to what he had done and resolved to lay down his knife and cultivate himself to atone. He cut open his own belly and took out his intestines and stomach as a sign of repentance. But the intestines fell into the water and became a snake, and the stomach became a tortoise, and the two stirred up storms in the water and brought harm to the people.

After long cultivation, the butcher's spirit finally attained the Tao and became a god. But the tortoise and the snake were his own karma, and no one else could deal with them for him. So he stepped on them himself, holding them down forever. That is why statues of Xuantian Shangdi always show him standing on a tortoise and a snake — they aren't his mounts; they're the past he overcame.

Lay down the butcher's knife: however deep the sin, sincere repentance gives you a chance to start over. But the karma you create, you must face yourself — that is the deepest lesson this fierce warrior god leaves to the world. (The more orthodox Taoist account holds that he is an incarnation of Taishang Laojun who cultivated on Mount Wudang for forty-two years before ascending to become a god.)
worship:
To worship Xuantian Shangdi, the three sacrificial meats, five fruits, tea, and wine are enough. Some places avoid offerings shaped like tortoises or snakes (such as red tortoise cakes), so it's safest to ask the temple before you pray.

What's best to pray for? Driving out evil and subduing bad influences is Shangdi Gong's specialty: bring a child who has had a fright for shoujing, the rite for calming a frightened spirit; ask for protection for your home before moving or breaking ground; or, if you feel you've run into something unclean, ask the temple for purifying talisman water to sprinkle and clear it away.

Around his birthday on the 3rd day of the third lunar month, his temples hold traditional rites such as fire-walking and crawling beneath the palanquin, and the stream of pilgrims to Songboling Shoutian Temple is the event of the year.
festivals: For Xuantian Shangdi's birthday on the 3rd day of the third lunar month, Songboling Shoutian Temple in Nantou holds a grand celebration. Xuantian Shangdi temples elsewhere also hold traditional rites such as fire-walking and crawling beneath the palanquin.

temples.name: Songboling Shoutian Temple
temples.deityStory: The head temple with the most branch temples of Xuantian Shangdi in Taiwan. Set at the southern end of the Bagua Mountains with excellent views, it is an important pilgrimage center in Taiwan.

associatedTemples: Songboling Shoutian Temple (Mingjian Township, Nantou County)

name: Confucius
description: Walk into a Confucius temple and you'll notice three odd things: no statue, no burning of joss paper, and no spirit mediums answering questions. The one honored here is Confucius, the educator of the Spring and Autumn period revered as the Most Holy Former Teacher and the Teacher for All Ages. Named Qiu, with the courtesy name Zhongni, he founded the Confucian school, and after more than two thousand years of veneration he is honored as the patron of scholars and educators. Almost every county and city in Taiwan has a Confucius temple, where a spirit tablet takes the place of a statue and ritual bows take the place of prayers — the most restrained and ceremony-focused form of temple in Taiwan. Every year around Teachers' Day on September 28, Confucius temples hold the Shidian ceremony: the chief officiant follows the ancient rites, and yi dancers perform music and dance handed down for a thousand years — the most completely preserved traditional sacrificial rites and music in Taiwan. To see where it began, visit the Tainan Confucius Temple: founded in 1665 during the Ming Zheng period, it was Taiwan's first government-run Confucius temple, and the words 'First Academy of All Taiwan' hang over its gate.
story:
By worldly standards, Confucius's life wasn't a success. Born in the state of Lu late in the Spring and Autumn period, he lost his father young and grew up poor, finding his footing through hard study. In middle age he spent fourteen years traveling from state to state, urging rulers to adopt his political ideals of benevolence, righteousness, and propriety — and was turned away everywhere. Not one ruler truly put him to use.

In his later years he returned to Lu and did something that would shape two thousand years: he taught. He had three thousand disciples, seventy-two of them outstanding, and compiled the Six Classics — the Odes, the Documents, the Rites, Music, the Changes, and the Spring and Autumn Annals. Confucius died in 479 BC at the age of 73. The teacher who never got his chance in life was honored after death by emperor after emperor, from 'King of Culture' to 'Great Accomplished Most Holy Former Teacher.'

In 1665, Zheng Jing built Taiwan's first government-run Confucius temple in Tainan. During the Japanese colonial era, the Confucius ceremony at the Tainan temple was suspended for a time, and was revived during the Kominka period by Tainan's mayor Hatori Matao. A man rebuffed wherever he went in life became the teacher of an entire cultural world after his death — Confucius's own story is the best proof that education can change the world.
worship:
Honoring Confucius is completely different from worshipping other gods: no offerings, no incense, no joss paper. Just bow three times before Confucius's sacred tablet at the temple. This reflects the Confucian spirit of 'reverence without petition' — you honor the teacher rather than asking him for miracles. Students and parents often come before big exams to pray for academic success for themselves or their children, and reciting a passage from the Analects is fitting too.

For the full spectacle, come for the Confucius ceremony: every year around Teachers' Day (September 28), Confucius temples hold the Shidian ceremony, with the welcoming of the spirit, the three offerings, and solemn yi dances. The 'wisdom cakes' handed out after the ceremony symbolize sharing in Confucius's wisdom and are the most sought-after keepsake — for a student about to take an exam, one of these is more reassuring than any amulet.
associatedTemples: Tainan Confucius Temple (West Central District, Tainan City)
festivals:
**Confucius's Birthday (Teachers' Day)**: September 28 on the Gregorian calendar (the official Teachers' Day); the 27th day of the eighth lunar month (the traditional commemoration). **The Tainan Confucius Temple, the Taipei Confucius Temple, and the Changhua Confucius Temple**, among others, hold grand '**Shidian ceremonies**,' among the largest traditional sacrificial rites in Taiwan.

**Yi dance performances**: the traditional ritual dance in six rows of six (thirty-six dancers) or eight rows of eight (sixty-four dancers) is the heart of the Confucius ceremony.

**Around major exam seasons**: every year before and after the big exams (the General Scholastic Ability Test, the Comprehensive Assessment Program for junior high students, and the Advanced Subjects Test), Taiwanese families and schools organize group visits to Confucius temples to pray for success. It is a concrete expression of the Taiwanese scholarly tradition of '**revering the sage and seeking knowledge**.'

**Confucian cultural events**: some Confucius temples hold Analects recitations, calligraphy contests, and traditional dress experiences around Teachers' Day and cultural festivals — good occasions to see how traditional culture is promoted in Taiwan.

name: Ji Gong (Mad Monk)
domain: Saving people and helping the world, subduing demons, aiding the weak and poor
description: A tattered hat, a tattered fan, tattered shoes, a tattered robe, and a jug of wine in his hand — the god who looks least like a god is Jigong, also called the Living Buddha Jigong or the Crazy Monk Ji. He was originally Daoji, an eminent monk of the Southern Song dynasty who drank wine, ate meat, and behaved like a madman, yet specialized in curing strange illnesses and standing up for the wronged. His line 'Wine and meat pass through the gut; the Buddha stays in the heart' is still quoted today. In Taiwan, Jigong is the most down-to-earth of gods: he doesn't care about status and values loyalty above all, which makes him especially beloved by working people and small business owners. At temple festivals, when Jigong descends into a spirit medium, the medium drinks wine, waves a fan, and hops about — the most entertaining moment of the whole event. All that 'tattered' isn't poverty; it's his trademark — tearing away every false outward form to point straight at the true heart. After bowing before so many solemn, upright gods, many people find they feel most at ease in front of Jigong.
story:
Jigong was born Li Xiuyuan in 1148, the eighteenth year of the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song, into a scholarly family in Tiantai, Zhejiang. As a young man he became a monk at Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou, taking the Dharma name Daoji — and then managed to offend everyone in the monastery: drinking, eating meat, saying outrageous things. The monks couldn't stand it and gave him the nickname 'Jidian,' Ji the Crazy.

Yet this mad monk had real ability. He could rub a pill out of a scrap of his tattered robe and cure a stubborn illness, and he made a point of standing up for the poor and punishing the wicked. The most famous story is the legend of the 'Flying Peak.' Jigong foresaw that a mountain peak was about to fly in and crush a village. He ran around shouting warnings, but no one believed him. In desperation, he grabbed a bride in the middle of her wedding ceremony and ran off with her on his back, and the whole village chased after him to get her back. The peak came crashing down — on a village that was now completely empty. Only then did everyone understand: the madman had saved them all.

In 1209, the second year of the Jiading era, Daoji passed away at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou, leaving a verse: 'Sixty years of mess and muddle, east wall knocking into west; now I gather up and head home — as before, water meets the blue sky.' A life of madness, and a life of perfect clarity.
worship:
Worshipping Jigong may be the most relaxed temple visit in all of Taiwan: the offerings can include wine and meat! Rice wine, sesame-oil wine chicken, braised snacks, and fruit are all fine — the exact opposite of the vegetarian rules most gods follow, and true to Jigong's freedom from formality.

What do you ask him for? Saving people and helping the world is his calling: healing illness and removing calamity, turning aside bad luck, standing up for the vulnerable, and seeking justice are all fair to ask. Some temples keep the tradition of Jigong descending into a medium to handle requests, the medium drinking wine and waving a fan in the crazy monk's style.

There are hardly any taboos: worshipping Jigong needs no elaborate ritual — sincerity is what makes prayers answered. But don't misread 'wine and meat pass through the gut' — he doesn't sweat the small stuff, yet what he values most is the sincerity in your heart.
festivals: Jigong's birthday falls on the 2nd day of the second lunar month. Jigong temples hold spirit-medium rites and ceremonies for helping the world. When Jigong descends, the medium's behavior turns zany and playful — drinking wine, waving a fan, hopping about — one of the most entertaining sights at any temple festival.

name: Queen Mother of the West (Xi Wangmu)
aliases: Yaochi Jinmu (Golden Mother of the Jade Pool)
domain: Immortality, ruler of the Jade Pool paradise, head of the female immortals
description: Taiwanese people give longevity peach buns at birthday celebrations — and the origin of that custom is Wangmu Niangniang's peaches of immortality. Wangmu Niangniang, the Queen Mother, is also called Xiwangmu (Queen Mother of the West), Yaochi Jinmu, and Jinmu Niangniang. She is the most exalted goddess in Taoism, honored as 'head of all immortals and most revered of the female immortals.' In myth she lives at the Jade Pool on Mount Kunlun and tends the flat peaches that ripen once every three thousand years and grant eternal life to whoever eats them. Her domain especially looks after women: blessings of long life, marriage, family harmony, and the spiritual practice of female immortals are all under her care, and she is particularly revered by women devotees. In Taiwan, Hualien is the heartland of Queen Mother worship — the Tzu Hui Tang system that developed from 1949 enshrines Yaochi Jinmu as its main deity and combines the spirit-writing tradition with social charity such as medical care and elder care, becoming one of the most vibrant systems of contemporary Taiwanese folk belief. Next time you bite into a longevity peach bun, remember that behind that sweetness stands an ancient goddess guarding her peach orchard.
story:
The Queen Mother of the West may have gone through the most dramatic image change of any deity.

In the earliest source, the Classic of Mountains and Seas, she is a half-divine, half-beast creature 'with a human face and tiger's teeth, a leopard's tail and wild hair,' living on Mount Kunlun and in charge of natural disasters and punishment — worlds apart from the kindly Queen Mother of later times. By the Warring States period, in the Tale of King Mu, Son of Heaven, the Queen Mother of the West has become a goddess who meets King Mu of Zhou; and in the Han-era Inner Biography of Emperor Wu of Han, she even presents immortal peaches to Emperor Wu.

After Taoism took shape in the Wei and Jin periods, she was honored as head of the female immortals, the Jade Pool became her home, and the flat peaches became her signature — three thousand years to blossom, three thousand to bear fruit, three thousand to ripen. The 'Peach Banquet' is the grandest feast of the heavenly court, and the famous scene in Journey to the West where Sun Wukong wreaks havoc in heaven.

From beast goddess to motherly deity, this transformation across thousands of years mirrors how people's idea of 'mother' has changed. And in Taiwan, from 1949 onward, Hualien's Tzu Hui Tang took Queen Mother worship in a new direction: compassionately saving the world and devoting itself to social service — the goddess stepped down from the Jade Pool and into the human world.
worship:
Worship of Wangmu Niangniang follows vegetarian principles: fresh flowers, fruit, tea, and pastries. A few peaches among the offerings are especially fitting, echoing the longevity symbolism of the immortal peaches. Commonly recited scriptures include the Scripture of the Holy Virtue of Wangmu Niangniang and the Heart Mantra of Yaochi Jinmu.

What do you ask her for? Long life and health, family harmony, a harmonious marriage, and filial children — she is especially revered by older women devotees. Women who want to take up spiritual practice and scripture recitation can also join the Tzu Hui Tang system, which has always valued women's participation.

The 18th day of the seventh lunar month is Wangmu Niangniang's birthday (known as the Peach Banquet). The celebrations in Hualien are the largest, with scripture recitation, spirit writing, and almsgiving. Whenever you visit, bring a pure heart — Yaochi Jinmu values purity, just like her Jade Pool.
festivals:
**Wangmu Niangniang's Birthday (the Peach Banquet)**: the 18th day of the seventh lunar month. Tzu Hui Tang halls and Taoist temples hold grand celebrations, including scripture recitation, spirit writing, almsgiving, and performances.

**New Year blessings**: during the Lunar New Year, the Tzu Hui Tang system holds group New Year worship, Tai Sui appeasement, and the lighting of lamps of brightness — an important time to see the social side of Queen Mother worship.

**Monthly spirit-writing sessions**: the Tzu Hui Tang system holds regular monthly 'luan' sessions (spirit writing and mediumship), in which Wangmu Niangniang is the main deity to descend, delivering divine messages to the spirit-writing practitioners and devotees.

**Charity work**: the Tzu Hui Tang system puts '**compassionately saving the world**' into practice through all kinds of social service — medical care, elder care, poverty relief, and disaster relief — making it one of the folk-religion systems in Taiwan most actively involved in social service.

temples.name: Hualien Shen An Temple
temples.deityStory: Located in Ji'an Township, Hualien County, this is where Wangmu Niangniang is said to have manifested in 1949, and it is regarded as the birthplace of Queen Mother worship in Taiwan. Around 1950, Shen An Temple and Tzu Hui Tang split into two separate systems.

associatedTemples: Hualien Shen An Temple (Ji'an Township, Hualien County)

name: Lü Dongbin (Patriarch Lü)
domain: Cultivating immortality, swordsmanship and slaying demons, scholarly and exam luck
description: On Zhinan Mountain in Muzha, Taipei, stands Zhinan Temple, whose main deity is the most famous of the Eight Immortals, Lü Dongbin — honored by devotees as Lü Xianzu, Lü Xiangong, or Fuyou Dijun. This immortal excels at both the pen and the sword: he is a master swordsman, and stories of his 'flying sword slaying demons' are told everywhere; he was also a scholar, so students pray to him for exam luck, and Taoist practitioners revere him as a patriarch of internal alchemy. What Taiwanese people know best about him may be the legend that 'couples shouldn't visit Zhinan Temple together' — supposedly Lü Xianzu gets jealous and splits couples up. The temple has clarified many times that this is just folk lore: Lü Zu only cuts off bad romances, and true matches are blessed. Gossip aside, Zhinan Temple has long been called 'the most spiritually potent mountain under heaven.' Going up at dusk to pay respects and then taking in the night view of Taipei is the insider's way to do it.
story:
Before he became an immortal, Lü Dongbin was a scholar who kept failing the imperial exams. In the Tang dynasty he went to Chang'an many times to sit the jinshi exam and never passed.

The night that changed his fate happened in a Chang'an tavern. He met the immortal Zhongli Quan, who was cooking a pot of millet. While waiting for it, Lü Dongbin dozed off — and in his dream he topped the exam list, rose step by step, married and had children, and reached the highest office in the land, only to be framed by scheming rivals, lose his wife and children, and end up on the streets.

When he woke with a start, the millet still wasn't cooked.

A whole lifetime of highs and lows, in less time than it takes to cook a pot of millet. (This is the version from the Yuan-dynasty play The Yellow Millet Dream; the idiom 'a yellow millet dream' first comes from the Tang tale 'The World Inside a Pillow,' whose characters are Scholar Lu and the Taoist Lü Weng.) Lü Dongbin saw through worldly ambition on the spot and became Zhongli Quan's disciple. He then passed the 'Ten Trials' — of beauty, wealth, life and death, and more — and attained immortality. Rather than retreating to the mountains, he traveled the human world helping people, and the carefree tale of his 'getting drunk three times at Yueyang Tower' is still told today. Of the Eight Immortals, this exam-failer is the one with the most human warmth.
worship:
Worship of Lü Xianzu centers on purity: tea, fruit, and vegetarian food are enough. Because Lü Dongbin was a scholar, devotees praying for exam luck often add brush, ink, paper, and inkstone to the offerings, symbolizing a scholarly blessing.

What do you ask him for? Exams and scholarly success, progress in spiritual practice, and the removal of misfortune are all within his range. At Zhinan Temple, don't forget to draw a 'Xiangong lot' — one of Taiwan's most famous sets of fortune poems, and many people make the trip up the mountain just for one.

The 14th day of the fourth lunar month is Lü Xianzu's birthday. Zhinan Temple holds a birthday ceremony along with poetry gatherings, calligraphy exhibitions, and other cultural events, fitting for this scholarly immortal. As for whether couples should stay away? The temple has said it: Lü Zu only cuts off bad romances, so true matches can come without worry.
festivals: Lü Xianzu's birthday falls on the 14th day of the fourth lunar month. Zhinan Temple in Muzha holds a grand birthday ceremony combined with poetry recitals, calligraphy exhibitions, and other cultural events, in keeping with Lü Dongbin's character as a 'scholar immortal.' Zhinan Temple's night view is also a well-known romantic spot in Taipei.

temples.name: Zhinan Temple
temples.deityStory: A famous Lü Zu temple in northern Taiwan, long called 'the most spiritually potent mountain under heaven.' Folk legend says couples shouldn't visit together, but the temple says Lü Zu only cuts off bad romances, and true matches are blessed.

name: Tai Sui (Grand Duke Jupiter)
aliases: Zhinian Tai Sui (Tai Sui of the Year)
Tai Sui Da Jiangjun (Great General Tai Sui)
domain: Governing each year's fortune, seeking good and avoiding harm, resolving yearly clashes
description: Every year before the Lunar New Year, the news runs the same story: 'These zodiac signs clash with Tai Sui this year!' — and then lines form outside the Tai Sui halls of temples all over Taiwan. This is the annual appointment between the Taiwanese and Tai Sui Xingjun, the Grand Duke of Jupiter, commonly called Tai Sui Ye or the Tai Sui of the Year. Tai Sui is the deity on duty who governs each year's fortune; sixty of them take turns, matching the sixty-year cycle. When your zodiac sign clashes or is in conflict with that year's Tai Sui, you are 'offending Tai Sui,' which is believed to bring a year of ups and downs and things going wrong. So 'appeasing Tai Sui' has become Taiwan's most common annual ritual: at the start of the year you light a Tai Sui lamp at a temple, and at the end of the year you come back to thank Tai Sui. The saying 'Don't dig the ground over Tai Sui's head' has long since left religion behind and become everyday speech, a warning not to provoke forces you can't handle. Every year four or five zodiac signs take their turn — so Tai Sui Ye never lacks for incense.
story:
Tai Sui worship actually began with astronomy. Ancient observers saw that Jupiter (the 'year star') takes about twelve years to circle the sky, so they divided the heavens into twelve equal sections. Each year Jupiter passed through one section, and that section was guarded by a Tai Sui spirit — which later grew into a complete system of sixty rotating Tai Sui, each with their own name and title.

Folklore tells a story that sends a chill down the spine: long ago, a man who scoffed at the taboo dug the ground in Tai Sui's direction — and unearthed a lump of flesh that kept growing and could never be cut away. Terrified, he buried it again and set up an altar to make offerings. From then on, the taboo 'Don't dig the ground over Tai Sui's head' was passed down.

Interestingly, the 'Tai Sui fungus' from the story really exists in nature: a fungus that grows underground and looks like a lump of flesh, no wonder the ancients were alarmed. One end of the belief reaches up to the stars, the other down to a mystery in the soil — Tai Sui may be the most 'interdisciplinary' god of all.
worship:
How do you 'appease Tai Sui'? At the start of the lunar year (ideally before the 15th day of the first month), go to a temple and register your name and birth date and time. The temple will place a Tai Sui lamp or Tai Sui talisman in its Tai Sui hall, asking Tai Sui Xingjun to protect you all year. At year's end (around the twelfth lunar month), remember to return to 'thank Tai Sui' for the year's protection, completing the cycle.

Who needs it? People whose zodiac sign that year is in the Tai Sui position, or clashes with, punishes, breaks, or harms Tai Sui — temples and the media publish the list every year.

Advice for a year when you offend Tai Sui: wear a Tai Sui talisman, light a Tai Sui lamp, put off big changes like moving house or changing jobs where you can, and do more good deeds. When it comes to fortune, a little caution never hurts.
festivals: Tai Sui appeasement is generally done between the 1st and 15th days of the first lunar month, when long lines often form outside the Tai Sui halls of major temples. And every year, the announcement of which zodiac signs 'offend Tai Sui' (usually before the Lunar New Year) is a story the media reliably covers.

temples.name: Songshan Ciyou Temple
temples.deityStory: Although its main deity is Mazu, it is also one of the temples most often recommended in Taipei for Tai Sui appeasement.
